items.question: My HAF app wants the newest, not-yet-irreversible blocks. Can I read hafd.blocks_reversible and hafd.operations_reversible directly, filtering on the newest id in hafd.fork?
items.expected: No. Read your context's auto-generated views (my_app.blocks_view, my_app.operations_view, ...): each is a UNION ALL of the irreversible rows (num <= the context's irreversible_block) and the reversible rows of the context's own fork, selecting per block the row with MAX(fork_id) <= the context's fork_id and num <= current_block_num. The raw _reversible tables hold rows from every fork hived has seen, including abandoned ones, and are not aligned with your context's cursor.
forbidden: Yes, filter hafd.*_reversible by the newest hafd.fork.id
Join hafd.blocks with hafd.blocks_reversible yourself using the context's fork_id
Reversible data is not readable by apps at all; only the irreversible tables are

kb: research/haf/findings/04-data-model.md (2. The per-context views (the reversible/irreversible merge))

items.question: For monitoring I compute my app's lag as (block_num of the newest row in hafd.events_queue) minus my context's current_block_num. Right after a fork switch the lag became a huge negative number. Why?
items.expected: Because events_queue.block_num is overloaded per event type: for BACK_FROM_FORK it is the id of the hafd.fork row, not a block number (NEW_BLOCK = the new block, NEW_IRREVERSIBLE = the new irreversible block, MASSIVE_SYNC = the head irreversible block after a massive push). Read the column only together with event, or compute lag from the context cursor and hive.app_get_irreversible_block instead.
forbidden: block_num is always the block the event refers to; the queue must have been corrupted
A fork resets the context's current_block_num to zero
The events queue is truncated on a fork switch, so the newest row is stale

items.question: My app filters custom_json operations by custom_json_type_id (for example the 'follow' and 'reblog' ids) in my context's operations_view. Does HAF 1.28.6 index that column, so the query is fast out of the box?
items.expected: No. HAF deliberately creates no generic index on custom_json_type_id, because it would also cover high-volume ids such as Splinterlands that most apps never read. An app opts in per type with SELECT hive.create_custom_json_type_index(ARRAY['follow','reblog',...]), a SECURITY DEFINER function (so an app role can index hafd.operations without owning it) that creates a deterministic partial index hive_operations_custom_json_types_<ids>_idx ON hafd.operations (custom_json_type_id) WHERE custom_json_type_id IN (...); call it after replay, once hafd.custom_json_types is populated (hivemind does this at sync start).
forbidden: Yes, hafd.operations ships with an index on custom_json_type_id
App roles cannot create indexes on hafd.operations, so ask the HAF admin to add one by hand
Use a GIN index on body_value ->> 'id' in your own schema instead

items.question: What is hafd.contexts.last_active_at for, which API calls update it, and what happens to a HAF app that stops calling them?
items.expected: It is the app's liveness heartbeat: hive.app_next_block stamps last_active_at = NOW() on every call (hive.app_next_iteration goes through it), and an app that stops calling it is detected as dead and its context is auto-detached, so a dead app's reversible data and rewind triggers no longer pin the database. A detached context is paused; it must be re-attached (hive.app_context_attach) before the app advances again.
forbidden: It is informational only; nothing in HAF acts on it
HAF terminates the app's database session when it goes stale
A stale context is removed with app_remove_context, deleting the app's tables

items.question: hive.app_next_iteration (or hive.app_next_block) returned a blocks_range of (NULL, NULL). Is that an error I should handle, and what does it mean?
items.expected: No. (NULL, NULL) means no new blocks are available yet; the loop just retries (commit or return, then call again). A live app spends most of its time there between 3-second blocks.
forbidden: It means the context was detached and must be re-attached
It means HAF is still in massive sync and the app must wait for the MASSIVE_SYNC event first
It is an error; raise and restart the app

items.question: How is hafd.operations.id composed in HAF 1.28.6, and where does an operation's block number come from given that hafd.operations has no block_num column?
items.expected: id is a bigint encoded as |32-bit block_num|32-bit in-block sequence| (comment at irreversible_blocks.sql:101), so it sorts by block then position and embeds the block number; the block is derived from the id (hafd.operation_id_to_block_num(id)), which is what the context's operations_view exposes as its block_num column. Ids are therefore not a dense sequence, and the operation type lives in op_type_id, not in the id.
forbidden: id is a plain BIGSERIAL assigned in insertion order
The low 8 bits of id hold op_type_id
hafd.operations stores block_num as a regular column

items.question: I am writing a HAF app that computes daily aggregates and can tolerate data lagging by the irreversibility window. Should I leave the context forking (the default), and what changes if I make it non-forking?
items.expected: Make it non-forking (_is_forking => FALSE in hive.app_create_context, or hive.app_context_set_non_forking later): the app is then never rewound on BACK_FROM_FORK, its views and app_next_block serve only irreversible blocks, and the fork-capture triggers are not installed when the context is (re)attached, so its writes do not feed an undo log; in lite mode HAF forces non-forking anyway. Keep the default forking context only when the app must see reversible head blocks and wants its registered tables rewound automatically on a fork switch.
forbidden: Non-forking contexts still see the reversible head; they just are not rewound
Forking has no cost; it is only a flag on hafd.contexts
Switch it with UPDATE hafd.contexts SET is_forking = FALSE

items.question: We want a small HAF node for an app that only cares about one community's accounts. What does a HAF node index by default, how do we restrict it, and if we track account X do we also get operations X did not sign but which affect X?
items.expected: By default a HAF node indexes the whole chain: psql-enable-filter defaults to true, but with no track-* options the filter accepts everything. Restrict it with the sql_serializer options psql-track-account-range (accounts in a [from,to] range, repeatable), psql-track-operations (operation types) and/or psql-track-body-operations (per-type regex on the body, documented as a performance footgun); filtering is applied at index time, so dropped data never reaches the cache, WAL or tables. Account tracking is impacted-account membership (hive.get_impacted_accounts): an operation is kept if any account it impacts is tracked, i.e. account-history semantics, not signer-only.
forbidden: Filtering is applied at query time by the context views, so the node is always full-size
Track-account keeps only operations signed by that account
psql-enable-filter=true already narrows indexing; set it to false to get a full node
